facts.fact: Saprolegnia is a filamentous water mould (oomycete) that normally feeds on dead organic matter but can attack damaged or stressed fish.
Saprolegniasis is caused mainly by Saprolegnia species, called water molds, which are common in fresh and brackish water.
Saprolegnia is a common cause of fungal infection in freshwater fish and fish eggs.
Even superficial skin or gill damage infected by fungus can be fatal if left untreated, so early diagnosis matters.
The mould secretes enzymes that break down fish tissue so it can absorb nutrients.
Infection is often first seen as fluffy, cotton-like tufts, white to gray or brown, on skin, fins, gills, eyes or eggs.
Tufts can turn brown or green as they trap sediment or algae; out of water they look like a slimy, matted mass.
Typically only one fish in the tank is affected.
Under the microscope, a scraping shows branching hyphae; the hyphae are broad and non-septate.
Affected fish may become sluggish, eat less and rub against tank walls or the pond bottom.

Columnaris is a bacterial infection that owners often mistake for fungus; its lesions are greyish or white patches that lack the body's shine and can turn brown or yellow, and mouth lesions may look like mould or cotton.
Saprolegnia often occurs together with columnaris bacteria or external parasites.
Infection is usually secondary to skin or gill damage from parasites, bacteria, viruses or injury.
Saprolegnia rarely attacks healthy, unstressed fish; risk factors include unhygienic water, overcrowding, skin injuries, poor diet and water temperatures below the fish's tolerance range.
Poor water quality (low circulation, low dissolved oxygen, high ammonia), high organic load and dead eggs are linked to infections.
Saprolegnia can grow at 32° to 95°F but prefers 59° to 86°F.
Primary infection of healthy fish happens less often and usually at low temperatures, possibly because immunity is reduced.
Spores resist drying and chemicals and are present in all ponds and tanks; fish mucus is thought to normally stop growth.
On eggs, Saprolegnia has difficulty colonising live eggs; unfertilised, damaged and dead eggs are infected first and it spreads from them to healthy neighbours.
Find and correct the reason the fungus took hold, because it rarely affects healthy fish.
Treat or correct predisposing factors at the same time as treating the fungus.
Once Saprolegnia is identified, evaluate and correct sanitation.
Topical treatment: clean the lesion with strong malachite green solution (100 mg/litre), then apply a waterproof cream.
Salt as a long-term bath at 1–5 g/litre, indefinitely.
Malachite green bath at 0.10 mg/litre, given as three treatments at three-day intervals.
Aquarium salt at 1–3 grams per litre, for salt-tolerant fish only.
Proprietary fungus remedies may contain malachite green or formalin; newer options include bronopol (Pyceze) and Pimenta extract (Pimafix).
Common treatments are potassium permanganate, formalin and povidone iodine solutions.
Overtreatment can further damage fish tissue and lead to recurring infections.
For eggs, methylene blue is the most widely used dye; the author suggests up to 3 ppm (3 mg per litre) through incubation.
For eggs, hydrogen peroxide (35%) at about 1 ml per 3.5 litres on day one, repeated on day two because it breaks down quickly; it is harsh.
Salt works against water moulds from about 3 ppt and suits fish adapted to hard, alkaline or brackish water; some fish will not tolerate even slightly raised salinity.
Carbon filtration absorbs treatments and treatments can harm the biological filter, so treat eggs in a separate container.
Chemicals react with organic matter, which lowers their effective dose.
Catfish can be extremely sensitive to salt.
Columnaris is treated with antibacterials such as acriflavine or Terramycin, not antifungals.
Bath in NaCl 2–3% for 15–30 minutes, or malachite green 0.1 ppm.
For sick farmed fish, bathe in formalin at 200–250 ml/m³ for about 30 minutes.
With eggs, remove unfertilised eggs quickly, and also remove eggs next to visibly infected ones.
Change salinity slowly, both when raising it and when lowering it.
Keep water quality and circulation good, avoid crowding (especially during spawning) to reduce injuries, and feed well.
Spores are almost always present, so prevention means managing conditions rather than eliminating spores.
Keep water clean, avoid overcrowding and remove decomposing organic matter.
Environmental management is essential to resolve chronic problems.
Before stocking, bathe young fish in 2–3% salt water for 5–10 minutes; avoid dense stocking.
Add vitamin C to feed at 200–300 g per 100 kg of feed.
Keep water quality good and avoid injuring fish.
Treating with chemicals but ignoring the underlying cause; fungus cannot be fully eliminated from a system.
Leaving carbon filtration running during treatment removes the medication.
Trying to save eggs already covered in established fuzz; they cannot be saved and should be removed.
Using cooler water against columnaris (a fungus look-alike) does not halt the disease.
In Vietnam the disease is reported in cá tra, cá basa, cá rô phi and cá trê, and is common in freshwater fish.
The disease thrives in the cold season or when water temperature swings irregularly.
The disease tends to occur when water temperature drops.
For ponds: after each crop, remove mud and apply lime at 7–10 kg/100 m²; lime twice monthly at 1.5–2 kg/100 m³ and before rain.
Practical Fishkeeping says it is wrong to call Saprolegnia a true fungus; it is an oomycete.
Practical Fishkeeping says the mould does not mainly kill healthy eggs; it takes hold on dead or unfertilised eggs first.
Malachite green is now used less because of restrictions in several regions, though some preparations still contain it.
